    The North Carolina exams

    North Carolina gives separate Life Agent and Accident & Health or Sickness Agent exams. Each has 55 scored, four-option multiple-choice questions plus up to 5 unscored pretest questions. Sections below follow the NC Department of Insurance content outlines (effective March 15, 2024).

    Life Agent examScored questions
    Types of individual life insurance17
    Annuities5
    Policy provisions, options and other features11
    Other life topics8
    NC statutes and regulations pertinent to life14
    Accident & Health examScored questions
    Accident & health insurance policies22
    Accident & health insurance provisions11
    Other accident & health topics8
    NC statutes and regulations pertinent to accident & health14

    About a quarter of each exam is North Carolina law. The rest is covered by the life and health topics that follow.

    Life insurance

    Insurers and how they are organized

    Test part A
    TermWhat it means
    InsurerThe company providing the insurance
    InsuredThe person covered by the policy
    Mutual companyOwned by policyholders. Issues participating policies: policyholders vote for the board and get dividends from divisible surplus
    Stock companyOwned by stockholders. Issues nonparticipating policies: no vote, no dividends
    Mixed planOne company issuing both participating and nonparticipating policies
    Fraternal benefit societyNonprofit, no capital stock, run solely for its members
    Reciprocal exchangeInter-insurance exchange: members insure one another
    SubscribersPeople who buy prepaid service plans

    Policy dividends are declared by the insurer and are never guaranteed.

    Reinsurance

    Reinsurance is insurance for insurance companies. It protects the insurer from catastrophic loss.

    • The ceding (original) insurer stays responsible to the client.
    • Treaty reinsurance is broad and automatic.
    • Facultative reinsurance is case by case, for specific risks.

    Where an insurer is incorporated

    TypeIncorporated in
    DomesticThis state
    ForeignAnother US state
    AlienOutside the United States
    Watch outThese types depend on where the insurer is incorporated, not where it sells policies or where an agent is licensed.

    An authorized (admitted) insurer holds a certificate of authority from that state's insurance commissioner (or director). Nonadmitted insurers write surplus lines coverage when authorized insurers won't accept the risk.

    Watch outA certificate of authority is the license a state gives an insurer to do business there. It is not a way for an agent to be licensed in one state and sell in another.

    Departments and people

    RoleJob
    Marketing / salesBring in new clients
    UnderwritingReview applications, investigate, classify risk, approve or decline
    ClaimsProcess, investigate and pay claims
    ActuarialSet rates, reserves and dividends using mortality and morbidity tables
    AgentRepresents one or more insurers under contract
    BrokerRepresents the insured rather than an insurer. Licensing rules for brokers vary by state
    SolicitorNot licensed to sell; introduces clients to a producer
    Service representativeSalaried employee who does no commissioned sales

    Two federal laws: the McCarran-Ferguson Act (1945) leaves insurance regulation to the states. The Fair Credit Reporting Act requires telling an applicant that their background is being investigated through a consumer report.

    Risk, loss and hazards

    Test part A

    Insurers cover only pure risk: a chance of loss with no chance of gain. Speculative risk, like buying stock, can lose or gain and is not insurable. A peril causes a loss; a hazard makes a loss more likely.

    HazardWhat drives itExample
    PhysicalA tangible condition you can see or measureIcy steps, faulty wiring, high blood pressure
    MoralDishonesty. IntentionalArson, faking a claim
    MoraleCarelessness because “I'm insured.” UnintentionalLeaving the car unlocked
    Watch outCareless or bad habits are morale hazard. Moral hazard always means intentional dishonesty.
    • Loss: an unintended reduction in financial value. A direct loss comes from the peril with no intervening cause. An indirect loss is a consequence of a direct loss, such as lost rent after a fire.
    • Accident: sudden and unexpected, at a specific time and place. Occurrence: any event that causes a loss, including gradual exposure. Every accident is an occurrence; not every occurrence is an accident.
    • Accidental means vs accidental results: “means” requires the cause to be accidental. “Results” (accidental bodily injury) only requires the outcome to be unexpected, so it covers more.
    • Lines of coverage: accident and health (illness, injury, disability), life (death), annuities (living too long), property (fire, wind, hail, theft, vandalism), liability (negligence, errors and omissions, third-party claims).
    • Named perils covers only the perils listed. Open (special) perils covers everything not specifically excluded.

    Risk management methods: STARR

    MethodMeaningExample
    SharingSpread risk among several partiesReciprocal exchange, risk pooling
    TransferShift risk by contractBuying insurance, hold-harmless clause, reinsurance
    AvoidanceEliminate the activity or hazardNot doing the risky activity
    ReductionLower the chance or size of lossA company safety program
    RetentionDeliberately keep the riskDeductibles, self-insurance
    • Law of large numbers: the larger the group of similar, independent exposure units, the more predictable losses become.
    • Exposure units must be homogeneous: similar objects exposed to the same perils.
    • Adverse selection: higher-risk people seek coverage more, so claims run higher than expected. Underwriting prevents it. Concealing material facts on an application is a form of it.
    • Indemnity: restore the insured to their pre-loss financial position, with no profit. Exceptions: life insurance, valued policies, replacement cost coverage.
    Watch out“As the number of insureds increases, the number of losses decreases” is a classic false statement. More insureds make losses more predictable, not fewer.

    Insurance contracts, agency and negligence

    Test part A

    A legal contract needs four elements, CLOC: Competent parties, Legal purpose, Offer and acceptance (agreement), Consideration. The applicant's consideration is the premium and the application statements; the insurer's is the promise to pay. STOLI (stranger-originated life insurance) fails legal purpose because the buyer has no insurable interest.

    Contract featureWhat it means
    AdhesionThe insurer writes it; the insured takes it or leaves it. Unclear wording is read in the insured's favor
    AleatoryUnequal exchange: one party may get far more than it paid in
    UnilateralOnly the insurer makes an enforceable promise. “Bilateral” is not an insurance term
    ConditionalConditions, like paying the premium and filing a claim, must be met before claims are paid
    • Representations are statements the applicant believes true. A material misrepresentation can void the policy. Warranties are statements guaranteed true.
    • Materiality: the insurer would not have issued the policy had it known the concealed fact. Rescission: the contract is treated as void.
    • Estoppel: the insurer can't deny a right it led the insured to rely on. It applies to a policy already in force. Parol evidence rule: oral statements made before the written contract can't change it.
    • Insurable interest: you would lose money if the insured died. For life insurance it must exist at application only, and it's presumed for yourself, a spouse, close family and business partners.

    Agent authority

    The principal (the insurer) is the source of all authority.

    TypeWhere it comes from
    ExpressWritten in the agent's contract
    ImpliedUnwritten, but needed to carry out the express duties
    ApparentThe public's reasonable belief, based on the insurer's words or actions

    Negligence

    LevelMeaningExample
    SimpleFailing to act reasonablyAgent forgets to submit a client's application
    GrossReckless disregard for acting reasonablyAgent consistently fails to keep client records
    Willful and wantonKnowing, deliberate disregardAgent knowingly processes a fraudulent claim
    Watch outImpersonation (someone else takes the medical exam for the applicant) and concealment (deliberately hiding a material fact) both let the insurer void the contract.

    Life insurance policies

    Test part B

    Term life is pure, temporary protection for a set period. It has the lowest premium per dollar of coverage and focuses on the death benefit.

    Term typeKey feature
    Level termFace amount stays the same; lowest premium for a limited time
    Decreasing termFace amount drops on a set schedule (mortgages, debts)
    Credit lifeDecreasing term that pays off a debt
    RenewableRenew without evidence of insurability; the new premium is always higher (attained age)
    ConvertibleChange to permanent coverage without evidence of insurability

    Converting at attained age uses your age at conversion, so the premium is higher. Original age uses your age when the term policy was issued.

    Permanent life

    PolicyKey feature
    Whole life (straight / ordinary)Permanent, level premium, cash value grows tax-deferred, pays no matter how or when the insured dies
    Limited-pay life (e.g. 20-pay)Lifetime coverage, but premiums stop early. Builds cash value faster than straight life. Coverage normally runs to age 100
    Single premium whole lifeOne payment; immediate cash value; usually a MEC
    Indeterminate premiumStates a maximum guaranteed premium but charges a lower current premium that the insurer can change
    Adjustable lifeOwner can change the face amount, premium and cash value
    Universal lifeTerm coverage plus a cash value account; flexible premiums
    Indexed universal lifeFixed (non-variable) product with interest tied to a market index
    Variable lifeCash value and death benefit rise and fall with separate-account investments; the owner bears the investment risk
    Joint and survivorInsures two people; pays at the second (last) death
    Industrial lifeSmall face amounts with premiums often paid weekly or monthly; some states cap the face amount (see your state's section)
    • Level premium concept: premiums in the early years are higher than the cost of protection. The excess builds the reserve that keeps later premiums level.
    • MEC (modified endowment contract): a policy funded too fast to pass the IRS 7-pay test, such as single premium. Loans and withdrawals become taxable; the death benefit stays tax-free.
    • Corridor: in universal life, the amount of pure insurance above the cash value.
    • Excess interest crediting: the index-linked method ties it to an economic index; the portfolio method ties it to the insurer's own investment earnings.
    • IOLI / STOLI: investors own a policy on someone unrelated to them, so there is no insurable interest.
    Watch outRaising the face amount with policy dividends (paid-up additions) is not adjustable life.

    How the premium is built

    • Three factors: mortality, interest and expense. Morbidity is not a life premium factor.
    • Net single premium = mortality cost − interest.
    • Gross premium = net premium + loading (the expense factor).

    More policy types

    • Endowment: pays the face amount at death during the term, or at the maturity date if the insured is alive.
    • Modified premium: lower premium for the first few years, then one step up to a higher level premium. Graded premium rises gradually each year before leveling off.
    • Jumping juvenile: the face amount increases automatically at a set age, often fivefold at 21, with no premium increase or proof of insurability.
    • Universal life is unbundled: mortality charges, expenses and interest credits are shown separately. The target premium is the amount the insurer suggests paying. Option A pays a level death benefit (the face amount includes the cash value); Option B pays the face amount plus the cash value.
    • Variable products are securities, so selling them also requires FINRA registration, such as the Series 6.

    Also on the exam outline High yield

    Policy types are the biggest section of the life exam. These are the details that show up in trickier questions.

    TermWhat to know
    Annually renewable term (ART)Renews every year without evidence of insurability; the premium rises each year
    Renewal age limitsInsurers stop renewals at an age such as 70 or 80 to limit adverse selection
    Decreasing termFace amount drops; the premium normally stays level
    Original-age conversionLower premium of the younger age, but the owner pays the premium difference plus interest back to the issue date
    Double protectionWhole life plus an equal amount of term to a set age: pays twice the face if death comes before that age. Not the same as double indemnity (accidental death)
    Family policyWhole life on the breadwinner, convertible term on the spouse and children. Newborns are added automatically with no premium increase
    Face amount plus cash valueBuilt by adding increasing term equal to the cash value
    Face amount plus return of premiumBuilt by adding increasing term equal to the premiums paid
    Joint lifeFirst-to-die: pays once, at the first death; costs less than two separate policies
    Survivorship (last survivor)Second-to-die: pays at the second death, often to pay estate taxes; lowest premium of the two
    Graded (limited) benefitLittle or no underwriting; pays a reduced amount for deaths from illness in the early years
    Interest-sensitive (current assumption) whole lifeFixed face amount; the premium or cash value changes with current interest and mortality results
    Universal life guaranteesA minimum interest rate and maximum mortality charges. Under Option A, the pure insurance shrinks as the cash value grows
    Variable universal lifeUniversal life's flexible premiums plus variable life's separate-account investments
    Watch outA 20-year endowment builds cash value faster than 20-pay life. Both stop premiums at 20 years, but only the endowment reaches the face amount then.

    Riders, provisions and options

    Test part B
    RiderWhat it does
    Waiver of premiumWaives premiums during total and permanent disability
    Payor benefitOn a juvenile policy; waives premiums if the payor (usually a parent) dies or is disabled
    Disability incomeMonthly income based on the face amount during total disability
    Accidental death benefitPays an extra sum if death is accidental
    Accelerated benefitsPays part of the death benefit early if the insured is terminally ill (1–2 years to live)
    Term riderAdds level or decreasing term coverage to a whole life policy
    ProvisionRule
    Entire contractThe policy, the application and any endorsements are the whole contract
    Insuring agreementThe insurer's promise to pay a stated sum
    IncontestabilityAfter 2 years, the insurer can't contest the policy's validity
    SuicideWithin 2 years of issue: premiums are refunded, no death benefit
    ReinstatementWithin a period set by state law, often 3 or 5 years after default (see your state's section). Needs a written application, evidence of insurability and overdue premiums with interest
    Automatic premium loanAn overdue premium is borrowed from cash value at the end of the grace period
    ExclusionsRisks the policy does not cover
    Absolute assignmentTransfers full ownership and control to the assignee
    Revocable beneficiaryThe owner can change them at any time
    Uniform Simultaneous Death ActIf no one can tell who died first, the insured is presumed to have outlived the beneficiary. Proceeds go to the contingent beneficiary or the insured's estate
    Common disaster clauseThe primary beneficiary must outlive the insured by a set time (often 30 days) or proceeds go to the contingent beneficiary
    Watch outUnder a common disaster clause, proceeds go to the insured's estate only when there is no contingent beneficiary.

    Nonforfeiture options

    These guarantee value even if the policy lapses.

    1. Cash surrender: take the cash value and end the policy.
    2. Reduced paid-up: a smaller face amount for life, with no more premiums.
    3. Extended term: the full face amount as term coverage for as long as the cash value lasts.

    Dividend options: CRAPO

    Cash, Reduction of premium, Accumulate at interest, Paid-up additions, One-year term.

    Taxes

    A lump-sum death benefit is free of income tax, but interest earned on proceeds held by the insurer is taxable. Cash value grows tax-deferred. Surrender value is the cash paid when the owner voluntarily ends the policy.

    More provisions

    ProvisionRule
    Grace periodUsually 30 or 31 days. Coverage continues, and an unpaid premium is deducted from a death claim
    Misstatement of age or genderBenefits are adjusted to what the premium paid would buy at the correct age
    War exclusionResults type excludes deaths caused by war; status type excludes any death while in military service
    Collateral assignmentPartial, temporary transfer to secure a loan; the lender is paid first
    Right to deferThe insurer may delay paying cash value or a loan (other than for premiums) up to 6 months
    Automatic nonforfeiture optionExtended term usually applies if the owner makes no election
    Guaranteed insurabilityBuy more coverage at set ages or events without proving insurability

    Settlement options (besides a lump sum): interest only, fixed period, fixed amount, and life income (single or joint). The owner chooses; if the owner didn't, the beneficiary can.

    Also on the exam outline

    ItemWhat to know
    Reinstatement advantagesKeeps the original issue age, values and terms. A new contestable period applies only to statements in the reinstatement application
    Change of planExchange the policy for another type with the same insurer; more pure insurance usually needs evidence of insurability
    Excess interestInterest above the guaranteed rate goes to the cash value or lowers premiums, but isn't guaranteed
    Withdrawal vs loanA withdrawal permanently lowers the cash value and death benefit. A loan accrues interest and can be repaid; any unpaid loan is subtracted from the death benefit
    Loan interestFixed (stated in the policy) or variable (adjusted against a published index)
    Other-insured riderTerm coverage on a spouse or children, added to the main policy
    Aviation exclusionExcludes pilots, crew and military or private flights; fare-paying airline passengers are covered
    DividendsA return of premium, not guaranteed and not taxable until they exceed premiums paid. Interest on accumulated dividends is taxable
    Premium modesAnnual costs least in total; monthly costs most. A front-end load comes out of each premium; a back-end load is a surrender charge
    Accidental death riderDeath must occur within 90 days of the accident
    Waiver of premiumAfter 6 months of total disability; premiums paid during the wait are refunded
    Waiver of monthly deductionUniversal life version: covers only the monthly cost of insurance and expense charges
    Cost of living riderRaises the face amount with inflation (often the CPI) without evidence of insurability

    Beneficiary designations

    • Per stirpes: a deceased beneficiary's share passes to their descendants. Per capita: it's split among the surviving named beneficiaries.
    • Class designation: a group such as “my children,” which includes children born later.
    • Estate: proceeds go through probate and can be reached by creditors.
    • Minors: name a trust, guardian or custodian, since a minor can't give the insurer a valid release.
    • Irrevocable: the beneficiary must consent before the owner changes them, takes a loan or assigns the policy.
    • Changing a beneficiary: the filing method needs only written notice to the insurer; the endorsement method needs the policy sent in to be endorsed.

    Underwriting, the application and delivery

    Test part A
    • Underwriting evaluates insurability and assigns a risk class: preferred (better than average), standard (the average baseline), substandard or rated (below average, extra premium), or declined.
    • The field underwriter is the agent, who starts the underwriting process.
    • Sources: the APS (attending physician statement) from the applicant's doctor; the MIB (Medical Information Bureau), which shares medical data among insurers; consumer (credit) reports, which show whether premiums will be paid on time.
    • Exam default: the owner, payor, applicant and insured are the same person unless the question says otherwise. If the insured is not the owner, every party signs. The applicant and the agent always sign.
    • Insurable interest must exist at the time of application for a valid life policy.
    • Discriminating against a protected class is illegal. Charging different rates for real risk differences is allowed.

    Receipts High yield

    Expect two to four exam questions on receipts.

    ReceiptWhen coverage startsWhere it's used
    ConditionalThe application date (or medical exam date), but only if the applicant qualifies as applied forMost common in life insurance
    BindingImmediately, until the insurer accepts or rejectsSparingly in life; mainly property and casualty

    If no premium is paid with the application, there is no coverage until the policy is delivered and the first premium is collected in full.

    • Free look: at least 10 days after delivery in most states to return the policy for a full refund. Some states allow longer, for example for seniors or mail-order sales (see your state's section).
    • Fiduciary responsibility: the producer holds premiums in trust and must act in the client's best interest.
    • Anti-money-laundering red flag: cash value paid out to a third party.
    • Master policy: issued to an employer to cover its employees in a group plan.

    Forming the contract

    • The application with the first premium is the applicant's offer. A policy issued as applied for is the insurer's acceptance; a policy issued differently (for example, at a higher premium) is a counteroffer the applicant must accept.
    • If no premium was paid with the application, the agent collects it at delivery along with a statement of continued good health.
    • Corrections on a paper application are crossed out and initialed by the applicant, never erased.
    • Cost comparison: the traditional net cost method (premiums minus dividends and cash value) ignores the time value of money. The interest-adjusted method accounts for it and is used in buyer's guide cost indexes.

    Annuities

    Test part C

    An annuity protects against living too long: it pays out a sum of money through regular payments. It's a contract between the contract owner and the insurer, and only a life insurer can guarantee income for the annuitant's whole life.

    PhaseWhat happensWho matters
    Accumulation (pay-in)Contributions grow tax-deferred; interest isn't taxed until withdrawnThe contract owner holds the rights; a named beneficiary receives the value if the owner dies
    Annuitization (payout)The first payment starts the payout; each payment is part principal, part interestThe annuitant receives income for a stated time or for life
    Annuity typeKey feature
    SPIA (single premium immediate)One premium; payments begin within 12 months
    SPDA (single premium deferred)One premium; payments begin later (at least 1 year)
    FPDA (flexible premium deferred)Periodic flexible premiums; payments begin after premiums stop
    Equity-indexedFixed (non-variable); interest linked to a stock market index
    MVA (market value adjusted)Also called a modified guaranteed annuity
    Life annuityPays for the annuitant's life, covering the risk of outliving savings

    Qualified plans are funded with pre-tax dollars: IRAs, 403(b) TSAs, 401(k)s and pensions often use annuities. Non-qualified annuities are bought with after-tax dollars.

    Payout options

    OptionWhat's guaranteed
    Straight (pure) lifeHighest income for one person; stops at death, nothing to a beneficiary
    Life with period certainPayments for life, and for at least the certain period (e.g. 10 years) even if the annuitant dies sooner
    Cash or installment refundAt least the amount paid in is paid out; the rest goes to a beneficiary in cash or installments
    Joint and survivorPayments continue until the second of two annuitants dies, sometimes at a reduced amount (for example, two-thirds) after the first death
    Joint lifePayments stop at the first death

    The longer the guarantee, the smaller each payment: life with a 20-year period certain pays less per month than life with 10 years, and straight life pays the most.

    Also on the exam outline

    • The annuity principle: life insurance creates an estate; an annuity liquidates one. Pooled mortality (annuitants who die early fund those who live longer) lets a life annuity pay more than interest alone.
    • Premium methods: single premium, or installments (fixed, flexible or periodic). An immediate annuity can only be bought with a single premium.
    • Who bears the risk: the insurer in a fixed annuity; the owner in a variable annuity. An indexed annuity guarantees a minimum rate and credits extra interest from an index, subject to caps or participation rates.
    • Variable annuity units: accumulation units during the pay-in period, converted at payout to a fixed number of annuity units whose value changes.
    • Guarantee before the annuity starting date: if the owner dies during accumulation, the beneficiary usually gets the greater of the premiums paid or the current value.
    • Surrender charges: a back-end load for cashing in early, usually shrinking each year.
    • Taxes on payments: the exclusion ratio makes part of each payment from a non-qualified annuity a tax-free return of the owner's cost basis.

    Taxes

    • Withdrawals before annuitization come out earnings first, taxed as ordinary income. Before age 59½, a 10% penalty applies unless an exception fits, such as death, disability or substantially equal payments (26 U.S.C. § 72).
    • Section 1035 exchanges are tax-free for life to life, life to annuity, and annuity to annuity, but not annuity to life (26 U.S.C. § 1035).

    Life insurance needs, business uses and retirement plans

    Test part C

    How much insurance? The human life value approach puts a dollar value on discounted future earnings and counts only lost income. The needs approach uses charts and tables to add up:

    • Lump-sum needs: final expenses, debt repayment, emergency fund, mortgage payoff, estate conservation, charitable gifts.
    • Income needs: support for survivors, education, retirement supplement, cash and liquidity.
    Business useHow it works
    Business continuation (buy-sell)Life insurance funds the agreement to buy out an owner who dies
    Key personThe business owns the policy, pays for it and is the beneficiary; the key employee is the insured
    Corporate-owned lifeIndemnifies the business for losses when operations are interrupted
    Split-dollarEmployer and employee share the cost; the employee names the beneficiary for their share
    Other usesEmployee benefits, reserve fund, business credit, favorable tax treatment

    Group life

    • The employer holds the master policy. It must be a natural group, formed for a reason other than buying insurance.
    • Conversion: an employee who leaves can convert to individual whole life within 31 days, with no medical exam or proof of insurability, at attained age, up to the group amount. If they die during the conversion period, the group policy pays.
    • Accidental death is not a type of group life policy.

    Retirement plans

    PlanKey point
    Defined contributionFunded by the employer, the employee or both
    403(b) TSATax-sheltered annuity for public school and 501(c)(3) nonprofit employees
    SIMPLE IRAFor small employers; simpler, with lower start-up and admin costs
    Keogh (HR-10)For the self-employed; allowed only if eligible employees are included

    ERISA requirements for qualified plans: a formal written plan, for the sole benefit of employees, meant to be permanent; eligibility at age 21 with 1 year of service; no discrimination in favor of highly paid employees; survivor benefits and minimum vesting; plan assets kept separate from the business.

    Vesting: employees are always 100% vested in their own contributions. For employer money in a defined benefit plan: 5-year cliff, or graded from 20% at year 3 to 100% at year 7. Example: Tom is 80% vested, so he forfeits 20% of the employer money.

    • Required minimum distributions start at 73. A missed RMD costs a 25% IRS excise tax.
    • An indirect rollover paid to you from a qualified plan, like profit sharing, has 20% withheld for income tax.
    • IRA rollovers are not limited by dollar amount.

    Buy-sell plans and the SEP

    • In a cross-purchase plan the business owners insure each other; in an entity (stock redemption) plan the business owns a policy on each owner.
    • A SEP (Simplified Employee Pension) puts employer contributions into each employee's own IRA with little paperwork.

    Social Security

    Test part C

    Social Security is OASDI: Old Age, Survivors and Disability Insurance.

    FICA High yield

    Who paysRate
    Employee7.65% (6.2% Social Security + 1.45% Medicare)
    Employer7.65% (matching)
    Self-employed15.3% (both shares)

    Social Security tax stops at a wage cap; Medicare tax has no cap.

    Insured statusRequirementWhat it gives
    Fully insured40 credits (about 10 years of work)Retirement and survivor benefits, premium-free Medicare Part A
    Currently insured6 credits in the last 13 quartersLimited survivor benefits
    Watch out“40 credits” is fully insured, not currently insured. Currently insured takes only 6 recent credits.
    • Disability: fully insured plus 20 credits in the 40 quarters before disability; a 5-month waiting period; total disability expected to last 12 months or end in death. Workers under 24 need 6 credits in the 3 years before disability.
    • Survivors: a $255 lump-sum death benefit, plus monthly income based on the worker's PIA. Children receive benefits until 18.
    • Blackout period: starts when the youngest child turns 16 and ends when the surviving spouse turns 60. No survivor benefits are paid in between.
    • AIME: average indexed monthly earnings, from the worker's highest 35 years adjusted for inflation. PIA: the full benefit at full retirement age.
    • Full retirement age: 65 for the oldest workers, rising to 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later.
    • Benefit period: the time frame for Medicare Part A hospital benefits.

    Producer ethics and unfair practices

    Test part A

    Every state bans the same core unfair trade practices. The details, penalties and deadlines are in your state's section.

    PracticeWhat it is
    TwistingMisrepresenting to get someone to drop a policy and buy another
    MisrepresentationKnowingly false or misleading statements about a policy, its benefits or the application
    DefamationMaliciously criticizing an insurer's financial condition
    ComminglingMixing premiums with personal funds. Premiums are held in trust (a fiduciary duty)
    Unfair discriminationTreating people in the same risk class differently for reasons unrelated to risk
    RebatingGiving anything of value not stated in the policy to induce a sale. Most states ban it, and some allow limited exceptions
    • Fair discrimination is allowed: charging smokers more than nonsmokers reflects a real difference in risk.
    • Replacement itself is legal when it's in the client's interest and the required notices are given. Twisting is replacement done through misrepresentation.
    • Controlled business is coverage written mainly on the agent's own family, employer or business.

    Health insurance

    Health insurance basics and limited coverage

    Test part D

    Health insurance has two main jobs: medical expense coverage pays for care, and disability income coverage replaces lost earnings.

    CoverageWhat it pays
    Medical expenseHospital, surgical, doctor and other costs of care
    Disability incomeA monthly benefit while the insured can't work
    Accidental death and dismemberment (AD&D)Principal sum for accidental death (and often loss of two limbs or both eyes); capital sum, a smaller set amount, for losing one limb or one eye
    Hospital indemnityA fixed amount per day or per stay, whatever the bill
    Specified (dread) diseaseOnly the diseases named in the policy, such as cancer
    Workers' compensationWork-related injury and illness; required by state law and paid for by employers
    • Accidental means requires both the cause and the result to be accidental. Accidental bodily injury (results) requires only an unexpected result, so it covers more.
    • Nonoccupational coverage excludes job-related losses because workers' compensation covers them. Occupational coverage pays on and off the job.
    • Common exclusions: intentionally self-inflicted injury, war, cosmetic surgery and losses covered by workers' compensation.

    Disability income insurance

    Test part D
    TermWhat it means
    Elimination periodWait after a disability starts before benefits begin; a longer one lowers the premium
    Probationary periodSickness that starts soon after the policy is issued isn't covered; applies once, to new policies
    Benefit periodThe longest time benefits are paid for one disability
    Own occupationDisabled if unable to do one's own job; the most favorable definition
    Any occupationDisabled only if unable to do any job suited to one's education, training or experience
    Presumptive disabilityLoss of sight, speech, hearing or two limbs counts as total disability even if working
    Partial disabilityA reduced benefit, often half, for a limited time
    Residual disabilityPays in proportion to the income lost after returning to work at lower pay
    Recurrent disabilityA relapse from the same cause within the policy's time limit continues the first claim, with no new elimination period

    Riders

    • Cost of living adjustment (COLA): raises benefits during a long claim to keep up with inflation.
    • Guaranteed insurability option: buy more coverage later as income rises, without proving insurability.
    • Social insurance supplement: pays when Social Security or another program pays less than expected, or nothing.
    • Waiver of premium: stops premiums during a long total disability.

    Business uses

    • Business overhead expense: pays rent, utilities and staff salaries while the owner is disabled. It doesn't replace the owner's income.
    • Disability buy-sell: funds the purchase of a disabled owner's share, often as a lump sum after a long elimination period of 1 to 2 years.
    • Key person disability: the business owns the policy, pays for it and receives the benefits.

    Medical expense insurance, managed care and the ACA

    Test part D

    Basic and major medical

    • Basic medical expense covers hospital, surgical and physician costs, often first-dollar but with low limits. Surgical benefits often follow a relative value scale or surgical schedule.
    • Major medical covers large expenses after a deductible, with coinsurance (such as 80/20). The stop-loss caps the insured's out-of-pocket costs; after that the plan pays 100%.
    • Supplemental major medical sits on top of a basic plan, with a corridor deductible between the two. Comprehensive major medical combines both in one policy with one deductible.
    • Common accident: one deductible when several family members are hurt in the same accident. Carryover: expenses in the last three months of a year count toward the next year's deductible.
    • Cost controls include preadmission certification and second surgical opinions.

    Managed care

    PlanKey features
    HMOPrepaid care in a service area; a primary care gatekeeper approves referrals; doctors often paid by capitation; emphasis on preventive care. A staff model (closed panel) employs its doctors; an IPA (open panel) contracts with independent doctors
    PPODiscounted network; out-of-network care is covered at a higher cost to the insured
    POSAn HMO-style primary care doctor, with PPO-style out-of-network coverage

    Affordable Care Act and tax-favored accounts

    • Children can stay on a parent's plan until they turn 26, even if they marry or live elsewhere (HealthCare.gov).
    • Individual plans can't refuse coverage or charge more for preexisting conditions.
    • Metal levels show the plan's estimated share of costs: Bronze 60%, Silver 70%, Gold 80%, Platinum 90%. Catastrophic plans are for people under 30 or with a hardship or affordability exemption (HealthCare.gov).
    • HSA: requires a high deductible health plan. Contributions are deductible, qualified withdrawals are tax-free, the balance rolls over, and non-medical withdrawals before 65 owe a 20% additional tax (IRS Pub. 969).
    • HRA: funded only by the employer. FSA: mostly use-it-or-lose-it.

    Health underwriting, taxes and business uses

    Test part D

    Health underwriting is about morbidity, the likelihood of sickness or injury. An impairment (exclusion) rider lets an insurer issue a policy while excluding one condition.

    CoveragePremiumsBenefits
    Individual disability income (paid with after-tax money)Not deductibleTax-free
    Employer-paid group disabilityDeductible to the employerTaxable to the employee
    Employer-paid group medicalDeductible to the employer; not income to the employeeTax-free
    Business overhead expenseDeductibleTaxable as business income
    Disability buy-sell and key person disabilityNot deductibleTax-free

    Health policy provisions and renewability

    Test part E

    Individual health policies use the uniform provisions: 12 mandatory and a set of optional ones. Each state adopts its own version, so check your state's section for its exact numbers.

    Mandatory provisionStandard rule
    Entire contractThe policy and attached papers are the whole agreement
    Time limit on certain defensesMisstatements (except fraudulent ones) can't void the policy after 2 years in most states (3 in some)
    Grace period7 days weekly, 10 days monthly, 31 days otherwise
    ReinstatementAutomatic if the insurer doesn't act on the application within 45 days; accidents covered right away, sickness after 10 days
    Notice of claimWithin 20 days of the loss
    Claim formsInsurer sends them within 15 days
    Proof of lossWithin 90 days in the standard provision (some states allow longer); no later than 1 year unless the insured lacked legal capacity
    Time of payment of claimsImmediately on proof; disability benefits at least monthly
    Payment of claimsTo the insured, or the beneficiary for death benefits
    Physical exam and autopsyInsurer may examine the insured during a claim, at its own expense
    Legal actionsNot before 60 days after proof of loss, and not after 3 years
    Change of beneficiaryThe insured can change it unless the designation is irrevocable

    Optional provisions include change of occupation (benefits adjust to the new job's risk), misstatement of age, other insurance with this or other insurers, relation of earnings to insurance (benefits limited to earnings), unpaid premium (deducted from a claim), cancellation, conformity with state statutes, illegal occupation, and intoxicants and narcotics.

    Renewability, from most to least protective

    1. Noncancelable: can't be canceled, and the premium can't rise, until a stated age.
    2. Guaranteed renewable: must be renewed until a stated age; premiums can rise only for a whole class.
    3. Conditionally renewable: can be nonrenewed only for reasons stated in the policy, never for health alone.
    4. Optionally renewable: the insurer can decline to renew on any anniversary or premium due date.
    5. Cancelable: the insurer can cancel at any time with notice.

    Group health and COBRA

    Test part E
    • Group coverage is underwritten for the group as a whole. The employer holds the master policy; each member gets a certificate.
    • Blanket policies cover a changing group, such as students or passengers, without naming them. A MEWA lets several small employers band together for benefits.
    • Coordination of benefits: the plan covering a person as an employee pays first. For children covered by both parents, the birthday rule makes the plan of the parent whose birthday comes first in the year primary.
    COBRA ruleFederal requirement
    Employers covered20 or more employees (states may have mini-COBRA laws for smaller ones)
    Job loss or reduced hours18 months
    Disability extension29 months, if Social Security finds the person disabled within the first 60 days
    Death, divorce, Medicare entitlement, child aging out36 months for spouses and dependents
    PremiumUp to 102% of cost (150% during the disability extension)
    ElectionAt least 60 days; first payment within 45 days of electing

    Source: U.S. Department of Labor COBRA FAQs.

    Medicare, Medigap and Medicaid

    Test part E
    PartCovers
    A (hospital)Inpatient hospital, skilled nursing facility, hospice and home health care
    B (medical)Doctors, outpatient care, durable medical equipment and many preventive services
    C (Medicare Advantage)Private plans that bundle A, B and usually D
    D (drugs)Prescription drugs

    Source: Medicare.gov.

    • Medicare covers people 65 and older, and people under 65 after 24 months of Social Security disability benefits or with end-stage renal disease.
    • Medigap policies fill Medicare's gaps. They're standardized: every company's plan with the same letter has the same benefits.
    • The Medigap open enrollment period is a one-time, 6-month window starting the first month a person is 65 and enrolled in Part B. During it, insurers can't refuse to sell or charge more for health (Medicare.gov).
    • Medicaid is a joint federal and state program for people with limited income and resources.
    Watch outMedicare doesn't pay for long-term custodial care. It covers only limited skilled nursing facility care.

    Long-term care

    Test part E
    • The six activities of daily living: eating, toileting, transferring, bathing, dressing and continence.
    • A tax-qualified policy pays when a licensed health care practitioner certifies, within the past 12 months, that the person can't do at least 2 ADLs for 90 days, or needs substantial supervision because of severe cognitive impairment.
    • A qualified long-term care contract is treated as accident and health insurance for taxes (26 U.S.C. § 7702B).
    • Levels of care run from skilled and intermediate care to custodial care (help with daily activities), plus home health care, adult day care and respite care.
    • Inflation protection raises the benefit amount over time.

    North Carolina law

    North Carolina law: life

    Test part F

    The Commissioner and licensing

    • The Commissioner of Insurance is elected by the people for four years. If the office becomes vacant, the Governor fills it for the rest of the term (G.S. 58-2-5).
    • A resident producer must be at least 18. The Commissioner can issue a temporary producer license, without an exam, for up to 180 days, for example after a producer dies or is called to military service. A nonresident producer is never required to have a resident producer countersign (Article 33).
    • Continuing education: up to 24 credit hours every 2 years. A producer who misses the compliance date has 4 months to finish, with a $75 reinstatement fee, before the license goes inactive. Nonresident producers have no NC CE requirement (NCDOI).
    DeadlineTimeSource
    Insurer files a new producer's appointment15 days after the first applicationG.S. 58-33-40
    Insurer reports ending an appointment to the Commissioner30 daysG.S. 58-33-56
    Insurer tells the producer15 days after notifying the CommissionerG.S. 58-33-56
    Producer responds to the Commissioner30 daysG.S. 58-33-56
    Licensee reports a criminal conviction10 daysG.S. 58-2-69
    Licensee reports a new home or email address10 business daysG.S. 58-2-69
    Licensee reports an administrative action in another state30 days after final dispositionG.S. 58-33-32
    Licensee reports a criminal prosecution30 days after the initial pretrial hearingG.S. 58-33-32

    Selling life insurance and annuities

    • Before a sales presentation, the agent must say they're a life insurance agent and name the insurer (G.S. 58-60-20).
    • The buyer gets the Buyer's Guide and Policy Summary before the insurer accepts the first premium, or with the policy if it has an unconditional refund provision of at least 10 days. The summary is titled “Statement of Policy Cost and Benefit Information.” Failing to deliver them counts as misrepresentation (Article 60).
    • Annuities: the disclosure document and buyer's guide come at or before application, or within 5 business days for other sales. If they weren't given at application, the buyer gets a free look of at least 15 days (G.S. 58-60-135).
    • Replacement: the producer presents and reads the Notice Regarding Replacement no later than when the application is taken. The applicant and producer both sign it, and a copy is left with the applicant (11 NCAC 12 .0605). Replacement includes lapsing, surrendering or converting an existing policy to reduced paid-up or extended term, or using it in a financed purchase (.0602).
    Watch outNC law has no general free-look period for individual life policies. The 10 days is the refund provision an insurer needs if it wants to deliver the Buyer's Guide with the policy. Annuities have the 15-day rule above.

    Policy rules

    RuleNC requirementSource
    Grace period (life)31 days for every premium but the firstG.S. 58-58-22
    Incontestability and suicide2 years from issue; suicide in that time returns at least the premiumsG.S. 58-58-22
    Reinstatement (life)Within 5 years of default, unless surrendered for cash; needs evidence of insurability and back premiums with interestG.S. 58-58-22
    Annuities31-day grace period; reinstatement within 1 year of defaultG.S. 58-58-23
    Lapse noticeIn the first year after default, no lapse until 30 days after a premium notice is mailed (not for monthly premiums, group, or term of 1 year or less)G.S. 58-58-120
    Industrial lifePremiums paid monthly or more often and a face amount of $1,000 or lessG.S. 58-58-5
    MinorsFull power to contract for insurance or annuities at 15 and olderG.S. 58-58-100
    Group life conversionWithin 31 days after a job ends. If the whole group policy ends: insured at least 5 years, up to $10,000G.S. 58-58-140
    Policy loan interestFixed rate up to 8%, or an adjustable rate set at least every 12 months but not more than every 3 monthsG.S. 58-61-10
    Guaranty association$300,000 for all benefits, including cash values, per lifeG.S. 58-62-21

    Unfair practices, fraud and privacy

    • Rebating (anything of value not in the policy, offered to induce a sale) is an unfair trade practice. Policy dividends on participating policies are not rebates (G.S. 58-63-15).
    • Unauthorized insurers: representing one unknowingly is a Class 1 misdemeanor; if the producer knew or should have known, it's a Class H felony. Either way the producer is strictly liable for unpaid claims (G.S. 58-33-95).
    • A producer who knowingly makes a false statement on an application, or to obtain a commission, commits a Class 1 misdemeanor (G.S. 58-33-105). A false statement to collect a claim is a Class H felony under $100,000 and a Class C felony at $100,000 or more (G.S. 58-2-161).
    • Privacy: pretext interviews are banned except in narrow claim-fraud cases. An authorization to collect information for a life application is valid for up to 30 months. After an adverse underwriting decision, the insurer gives specific reasons within 21 business days of a written request (Article 39).

    North Carolina law: health

    Test part G

    The licensing, unfair practices, fraud and privacy rules in the life section apply to health producers too. These are the health-specific rules.

    Required policy provisions

    NC's version of the uniform provisions is in G.S. 58-51-15.

    ProvisionNC requirement
    Time limit on certain defenses2 years from issue or reinstatement; a preexisting-condition period in this provision can't exceed 1 year
    Grace period7 days for weekly premiums, 10 for monthly, 31 for all others
    ReinstatementAccidents covered right away; sickness only if it begins more than 10 days after reinstatement
    Notice of claimWithin 20 days after the loss starts
    Claim formsInsurer sends them within 15 days, or the insured can send proof in their own words
    Proof of lossWithin 180 days after the loss, and no later than 1 year after that unless the insured lacked legal capacity
    Time of payment of claimsPeriodic benefits at least monthly; others immediately on due proof
    Legal actionsNot before 60 days after proof of loss, and not after 3 years from when proof was required
    Watch outNC gives 180 days for proof of loss, not the 90 days in the standard model provision.

    Who's covered

    • An individual or family hospitalization policy must let the buyer return it within 10 days for a full refund (G.S. 58-51-10).
    • Newborns are covered from the moment of birth. If adding the child costs extra, enroll within 30 days of birth. Adopted and foster children are covered from placement on the same 30-day terms (G.S. 58-51-30).
    • A dependent child whose disability prevents self-supporting work stays covered past the age limit. Proof is due within 31 days of reaching that age, then no more than once a year (G.S. 58-51-25).
    • Policies must cover a screening mammogram every year from age 50, every other year at 40–49, and one baseline at 35–39, plus cervical cancer screening (G.S. 58-51-57).
    • Long-term care premiums can rise at most 25% for a policyholder in one calendar year (G.S. 58-51-95).

    Group health: continuation, conversion and notice

    RuleNC requirement
    Eligibility for state continuationContinuously insured for the 3 months before coverage ended
    LengthUp to 18 months
    PremiumNo more than 102% of the group rate
    Time to electAt least 60 days
    Conversion after continuation endsApply within 31 days, no evidence of insurability

    Source: G.S. Chapter 58, Article 53. State continuation sits alongside federal COBRA, which covers employers with 20 or more employees.

    • An employer that stops paying group health premiums must give covered people at least 45 days' written notice before coverage ends. Willfully failing to is a Class H felony when losses are under $100,000 and a Class F felony at $100,000 or more (G.S. 58-50-40).
